Q: How to check a `struct gps_data_t*` for a NULL value the safe way? A:

Another potential point of failure is this:

tmc* tmc::Initialize()

Unless Initialize is a static member function of tmc, if the tmc instance is invalid, then anything you do in Initialize is also invalid.

The tell-tale sign of an invalid instance is either

  1. this is a null pointer or
  2. this is an invalid pointer or
  3. If this "looks ok", very simple function calls, assignments, etc. that are basically guaranteed to work in general, just fail. This really indicates that this just "looked ok", but is really invalid.

We need to see exactly how the instance of the class (in this case tmc) was created and how it is maintained.

Q: How to scroll the viewport so that the current line (prompt) moves to the top in WezTerm, similar to the effect of Ctrl+L in Windows PowerShell? A:

I'm a complete beginner, so please bear with me. I previously confused the concepts of terminal emulator, shell, and prompt customizer. After some research, I now understand:

  • A terminal emulator is a graphical program that provides a window for users to interact with a shell. It handles keyboard input, displays text output, manages multiple tabs, sets font colors, etc. Common examples include WezTerm.

  • A shell is a command-line interpreter that runs inside a terminal emulator. It accepts and executes user commands, and also serves as a scripting language for automation tasks. Common examples include PowerShell.

  • A prompt customizer is a plugin or theme system installed within a shell to replace the default simple prompt with a more attractive and informative one. Common examples include Oh My Posh and Starship.

Now that I've clarified these concepts, I realize the solution to my problem is straightforward: if I change the default shell used by WezTerm from CMD to PowerShell (either version 5.1 or 7+), then pressing Ctrl+L will clear the screen while preserving scrollback history, achieving the desired behavior.

Q: Mode for _mm_cmpistrm SSE4.2 intrinsic A:

For _SIDD_BIT_MASK you'll get a mask that is all 1 if the strings are equal and all 0 if they are unequal; if you're doing a _SIDD_UBYTE_OPS then you'll get 16 bits returned (one for each character in the string).

With _SIDD_UNIT_MASK however you'll get the same mask but expanded to 16 bytes instead. Eg bits 0..15 will all be 1 if the comparison of the first two characters in the string is true. And bits 16..31 for character two etc.

Q: Provenance of pointer fields of structs obtained from `std::ptr::read` over a buffer coming from the C FFI A:

The compiler has to assume exposed provenance unless you used the strict provenance APIs (which you likely should not for a C allocated object).

So your code will work assuming that the pointer points to some valid C object or a valid Rust allocation that has been exposed.

Q: How can I compare the contents of two text files in Python? A:

first read all lines of files

with open('file1.txt') as f1:
    a = f1.readlines()
with open('file2.txt') as f2:
    b = f2.readlines()

for reading files in python 3.10 or higher

with (
    open('file1.txt') as f1,
    open('file2.txt') as f2,
):
    a = f1.readlines()
    b = f2.readlines()

and now for print differences between file a and b

import difflib
a_sample = a[0] # 'New York Los Angeles Miami'
b_sample = b[0] # 'New York Orlando Miami Dc'
diff = difflib.ndiff(a.replace(' ', '\n').splitlines(keepends=True), b.replace(' ', '\n').splitlines(keepends=True))
print(''.join(diff), end="")
  New
  York
+ Orlando
- Los
- Angeles
- Miami+ Miami
?      +
+ Dc

and iterate all the files:

for file1_line, file2_line in zip(a, b):
    diff = difflib.ndiff(
                  a.replace(' ', '\n').splitlines(keepends=True), 
                  b.replace(' ', '\n').splitlines(keepends=True)
           )
    print(''.join(diff), end="")

What's the meaning difflib symbols:

code meaning
'- ' line unique to sequence 1
'+ ' line unique to sequence 2
' ' line common to both sequences
'? ' line not present in either input sequence

Note: you can iterate in diff output and print only + or - words.

python document: https://docs.python.org/3/library/difflib.html
